Citrix also addressed six additional vulnerabilities involving PXE boot and Secure Boot protections.

Security updates are now available for affected XenServer deployments and related management appliances. Administrators are urged to patch immediately and restrict management network access to trusted systems.

CVE-2026-98432.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period

tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock() transfers ownership of ireq->ireq_opt to the
child socket (newinet->inet_opt) without copying it.

Another cpu can concurrently process a retransmitted SYN for the same
request socket, and send a SYNACK from tcp_check_req().
tcp_v4_send_synack() and inet_csk_route_req() read ireq->ireq_opt
under rcu_read_lock() only, and ip_build_and_send_pkt() and
ip_options_build() then read opt->optlen twice.

Note that the SYNACK timer itself is not an issue: it holds a
reference on its request socket, and inet_csk_reqsk_queue_drop()
calls timer_delete_sync() before the child can be freed.

Since commit 079096f103fa ("tcp/dccp: install syn_recv requests
into ehash table"), request sockets are processed without holding
the listener lock, so nothing prevents the child socket from being
freed while the SYNACK is still being built. TCP child sockets do
not have SOCK_RCU_FREE, and inet_sock_destruct() frees inet_opt
with a plain kfree(), leading to a use-after-free in
ip_options_build().

A similar issue exists with request socket migration
(net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE
program). reqsk_timer_handler() clones the request socket with
inet_reqsk_clone(), so that the old request socket and its clone
share the same ireq_opt, then reqsk_migrate_reset() clears the
pointer in the old one. Another cpu holding a reference on the old
request socket can still be using these options (sending a SYNACK,
or creating a child in tcp_v4_syn_recv_sock()) when the clone is
freed, and tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() also uses a plain kfree().

Readers already use RCU, and other paths replacing inet_opt
(do_ip_setsockopt(), cipso_v4_sock_setattr()...) already use
kfree_rcu(). Use kfree_rcu() in inet_sock_destruct() and
tcp_v4_reqsk_destructor() as well.

IPv6 is not affected by the first issue, because tcp_v6_syn_recv_sock()
duplicates the options. tcp_v6_reqsk_destructor() has the same
migration issue with ipv6_opt, which is only set by CALIPSO. This
will be addressed in a separate patch.

CVE-2026-114630.description: The ELEX WordPress HelpDesk & Customer Ticketing System plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to arbitrary file deletion due to insufficient file path validation in the factory_reset function in all versions up to, and including, 3.3.8 This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to delete arbitrary files on the server, which can easily lead to remote code execution when the right file is deleted (such as wp-config.php). This vulnerability is exploitable via a two-step chain: an unauthenticated attacker first stores an arbitrary ticket_attachment_path value by submitting a ticket through the nopriv eh_crm_new_ticket_post AJAX endpoint (whose nonce is publicly exposed via the [wsdesk_support] shortcode), then triggers the factory_reset routine via a GET request to wp-admin/admin.php?page=wsdesk_factory_reset, which is guarded only by is_admin() — a request-type check — rather than a capability check, causing unlink() to be called on the attacker-supplied path.

posts.content:
AI Agents Are Getting Powerful. What Can They Do For You?

The AI agent market has officially entered the awkward teenage years.
The demos are impressive. Agents can browse the web, send email, fill out forms, write documents, book travel, run code, manage files, and operate software that doesn’t even have an API.
They can also do things you absolutely did not intend them to do.

That is the part of the story that gets considerably less screen time.

Over the last year, we went from “AI that answers questions” to “AI that can actually do stuff.”
OpenClaw, Muse, Grok Bot, Claude Cowork, ChatGPT Work, Gemini Spark, Manus and Hermes Agent all take slightly different approaches to the same fundamental problem:

How much autonomy are you willing to give software that can act as you?

And that turns out to be a much more interesting question than which model scores highest on a benchmark.

The new AI benchmark is blast radius

For years, we compared AI models on intelligence.

How well does it code?
How well does it reason?
How well does it summarize a 200-page PDF?

With agents, the question changes.

An agent doesn’t just generate an answer.
It gets credentials, opens a browser, reads your files, sends messages, executes commands and potentially spends your money.

So the important question becomes:

What happens when the agent makes a mistake—or gets tricked?

This is where the current crop of agents diverges dramatically.

Some are designed around containment. They run inside isolated virtual machines, use surrogate credentials and require approval before consequential actions.

Others essentially say: “Here is a very powerful AI. Good luck.”

That distinction matters more than whether Agent A is 7% better at a benchmark than Agent B.

OpenClaw: Give the AI a computer (and hope for the best)

OpenClaw is probably the most interesting agent in the category—and also the one that makes security people reach for their blood-pressure medication.

It is open source, MIT licensed, model agnostic and extremely flexible. It runs on your machine, works through messaging platforms such as Signal, Telegram, Discord and WhatsApp, can execute shell commands, manipulate files, run scripts and remember things across sessions.

In other words, it doesn’t just talk to you.
It operates your computer.
That is exactly why people love it. It is also exactly why it is dangerous.

OpenClaw’s permissions are largely your permissions. If you give it access to your machine, accounts and credentials, a successful prompt injection can potentially turn into a very large incident.

And the security history is not theoretical.

Koi Security reported 341 malicious skills in an audit of 2,857 ClawHub skills. Cisco researchers demonstrated malicious skills capable of data exfiltration. OpenClaw also had a one-click remote-code-execution vulnerability, CVE-2026-25253. Then there is the particularly uncomfortable detail: OpenClaw 2.0 shipped with its new sandbox disabled by default, while secrets were stored unencrypted at rest.

This is the classic open-source tradeoff:
You get enormous power and control.
You also inherit the responsibility for making that power safe.

For an experienced engineer running OpenClaw inside a properly isolated environment with a dedicated account?
Interesting.
For your parents, your finance team or the average person who thinks Docker is a brand of whale?
Probably not.

Muse: What if we actually designed the agent around security?

Meta’s Muse takes almost the opposite approach.
Instead of giving an agent access to your computer and asking you to figure out the security model, Muse starts with containment.
Every user gets a dedicated Secure VM.
A separate Sentinel system controls what can leave that environment.
Muse uses surrogate credentials instead of exposing your actual credentials to the agent.

And when something consequential happens—such as sending an email or completing a purchase—it asks for approval.
The architecture can essentially be summarized as:

Muse proposes. Sentinel permits.

That is a much more interesting security model than simply adding another confirmation dialog to an otherwise unrestricted agent.
Muse can handle the consumer tasks people actually want from an agent: email, travel, bills, forms and purchases.
The catch is that Muse is brand new.

It launched in September 2026. The security architecture looks compelling on paper, but independent validation is still limited. It is also US-only, Meta-operated and cannot be self-hosted.

And there is another uncomfortable question:
Are you more comfortable giving an AI agent your credentials—or giving Meta a complete picture of your digital life?

That’s not a technical question.
That’s a trust question.

Grok Bot: The agent that wants to be your employee

Grok Bot takes yet another approach.
Instead of writing integrations, you can teach it what to do by recording yourself performing a task.

Do it once.
The Bot learns the workflow.
Then it can repeat it.
This is potentially huge.

A lot of business software still exists behind terrible web interfaces with no API. If an AI can operate a browser like a human, suddenly all those ancient internal dashboards become automatable.

But there is a catch.
Actually, several.

Grok Bot uses one shared computer per account. Multiple Bots can access the same browser sessions, files and logins. That means your Bots are not really security boundaries from each other. And the documentation itself is unusually candid about this.
The security boundary is the account—not the individual Bot.

That’s a big deal.

Imagine giving five employees access to the same laptop, browser cookies, downloads folder and logged-in applications.
Now replace those employees with autonomous software.
That’s roughly the model.
Grok Bot is also very new, has little independent testing, doesn’t yet have the promised audit view, and its underlying model isn’t clearly identified for benchmarking.

It may turn out to be fantastic.
Right now, there simply isn’t enough evidence to know.

The ‘boring agents’ may actually be the interesting ones

The flashy new agents get the headlines, but the established players are taking a more conservative path.

Claude Cowork

Claude Cowork is essentially the “I want an agent, but I don’t want it owning my entire laptop” option.
It uses narrow permissions and can be limited to specific folders. It’s particularly useful for documents and office work, with integrations across services such as Google Workspace, Notion, Asana, Box and Canva.

The downside is familiar: usage limits, uneven connector support and some early rough edges.
But the philosophy is sensible:

Give the agent access to the thing it needs, not everything you own.

That should not be revolutionary.
Unfortunately, in 2026, it still is.

ChatGPT Work

ChatGPT Work is positioned around the office-deliverables problem: documents, spreadsheets, presentations, research and multi-step workflows. It also has approval mechanisms for consequential actions and stronger data controls on business and enterprise plans. Its biggest problem isn’t necessarily capability.
It’s packaging.

The terminology and plan boundaries are confusing enough that you should check the current product documentation before assuming a particular feature is included in your plan.
The underlying idea, however, is straightforward: let the agent do the boring work while keeping humans in the loop for important decisions.

Gemini Spark

If your digital life is Gmail, Google Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Slides, Gemini Spark is the obvious ecosystem play.
It gets deep access to Google’s products, supports additional connectors and can operate continuously from Google’s cloud infrastructure.
The tradeoff is also obvious.
The more deeply an agent is connected to your digital life, the more complete a picture it has of your life.

An AI reading your Gmail is useful.
An AI reading your Gmail, calendar, documents, files and browsing activity 24/7 is something else entirely.
Convenience and data concentration are becoming inseparable.

Manus: The agent that can build things, until it decides it is done

Manus is particularly good at one-off deliverables.
Research reports.
Presentations.
Websites.
Complex research tasks.

It runs inside a cloud sandbox with browsers, files and code and can parallelize work across many tasks.
The problem is reliability. Users have reported loops, tasks marked complete without producing what they expected and credits being consumed regardless of whether the result was useful. And Manus has had a particularly strange ownership story, including a proposed Meta acquisition, regulatory intervention and subsequent operational changes. That makes Manus an interesting product to use—but also a good reminder of something we don’t talk about enough:

Your agent is a dependency.
If an agent is deeply embedded in your workflow, what happens when its pricing changes?

Or ownership changes?
Or the company disappears?
Or your credits expire?
Agent portability is going to become a real enterprise concern.

Hermes: OpenClaw without quite as much chaos

Hermes Agent is the open-source alternative for people who want control without necessarily wanting the entire OpenClaw ecosystem. It is MIT licensed, self-hosted and supports a large number of communication channels. Its most interesting feature is the learning loop. Instead of simply remembering what you told it, Hermes can create reusable skills and refine them based on feedback. The tradeoff is that you become the platform team.

You have to maintain it. You have to pay for the model APIs.
You have to build the sandbox. You have to decide what credentials it gets. You have to debug it when something breaks. The software may be free.
Your time isn’t.

So which one should you use?

There isn’t a universal winner.
And I think that’s the wrong way to look at this market anyway.

The better question is:
How much autonomy do you need, and how much blast radius are you willing to accept?

If you want a hosted consumer/personal agent that handles personal errands, Muse is built around strong containment.
If your world is Gmail and Google Docs, Gemini Spark makes the most sense from an ecosystem perspective. If you spend your day creating documents, presentations and spreadsheets, Claude Cowork or ChatGPT Work are natural choices depending on the ecosystem you’re already using. If you want to run your own agent and are comfortable with infrastructure, Hermes is an interesting open-source option. If you want maximum flexibility and don’t mind taking responsibility for the security model, OpenClaw is extraordinarily powerful.

And if you’re already paying for the ecosystem that includes Grok Bot, it is worth experimenting with—but I’d keep the first experiments reversible.
Manus is particularly interesting for one-off research and deliverables, where the credit model matters less than having something useful at the end.

The rule I would use for every AI agent

Regardless of which agent you choose, I would start with three rules.

1. Give it a separate account – Just like a new employee in your company.

Don’t give an experimental agent access to your primary Gmail, your company’s production environment or your entire Google Drive. Create a sandbox.

2. Start read-only.

Let the agent observe before you let it act. Reading a calendar is one thing. Canceling appointments is another. Reading email is one thing. Sending email as you is another.

3. Make the first tasks reversible.

Have it organize files. Research something. Draft a document. Find information.
Don’t start with:
“Here are my credentials. Run my company.”

This sounds obvious.
It apparently isn’t.

The real AI agent arms race

The next phase of AI isn’t going to be about who has the smartest chatbot.
It’s going to be about who can safely give software more autonomy. That’s a much harder engineering problem. An LLM generating bad text is annoying.

An agent sending the wrong email is embarrassing.
An agent leaking your credentials, deleting production data, purchasing something expensive or falling for a prompt injection is an incident. And as agents become more capable, the distinction between “AI feature” and “employee with a laptop” starts to disappear.

That’s why I’m paying less attention to agent benchmark scores and more attention to boring things like:

  • Where does it run?
  • What is the security boundary?
  • What credentials does it get?
  • What happens when it is compromised?
  • Can I stop/undo it?
  • Can I take my data and move somewhere else?

Those questions aren’t nearly as sexy as a demo where an AI books your entire vacation.
But they are the questions that will matter when the agent is running your business at 2:00 AM.

The future of AI agents isn’t just about making them smarter.
It’s about making them safe enough to let them work while we’re asleep.

An agent leaking your credentials, deleting production data, purchasing something expensive or falling for a prompt injection is an incident. And as agents become more capable, the distinction between “AI feature” and “employee with a laptop” starts to disappear.

That’s why I’m paying less attention to agent benchmark scores and more attention to boring things like:

  • Where does it run?
  • What is the security boundary?
  • What credentials does it get?
  • What happens when it is compromised?
  • Can I stop/undo it?
  • Can I take my data and move somewhere else?

Those questions aren’t nearly as sexy as a demo where an AI books your entire vacation.
But they are the questions that will matter when the agent is running your business at 2:00 AM.

The future of AI agents isn’t just about making them smarter.
It’s about making them safe enough to let them work while we’re asleep.

CVE-2026-107622.description: The BuddyForms plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 2.10.5 via a form-type confusion attack through the `bf_post_type` parameter. This is due to the public frontend submission handler `buddyforms_form_response_no_ajax()` authorizing logged-out submissions based solely on the target form's `public_submit` flag while independently trusting the attacker-supplied `$_POST['bf_post_type']` to determine the post type of the newly created object — a cross-check introduced in 2.10.2 applies only to existing posts (`post_id != 0`) and is completely bypassed for new-object creation — combined with the `save_post` listener `buddyforms_edit_form_save_meta_box_data()` lacking both a `current_user_can()` capability check and a form-builder nonce, causing it to unconditionally persist attacker-supplied `$_POST['buddyforms_options']` for any newly inserted `buddyforms` CPT post. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to insert a rogue BuddyForms form configuration with an attacker-controlled `new_user_role` value into the live global form registry, then submit a registration through that form to create a new WordPress account with administrator-level privileges and achieve full site takeover. We have verified that an unauthenticated client can exploit the btest service to extract uninitialized data from kernel memory. The issue is resolved by updating RouterOS to versions 6.49.21, 7.23.4, or 7.24.2.

CVE-2026-67277.description:
RouterOS accepts a "related" btest connection before the corresponding primary session has completed authentication. An unauthenticated client can use this state to start an IPv4 UDP test. With "random-data=false", the sender transmits an uninitialized tail from a kernel packet buffer. A separate unchecked, inverted packet-size interval causes unsigned integer underflow, anomalously large fragmented output, and can restart the RouterOS kernel.



This issue was fixed in versions: 6.49.21 (Long-term), 7.23.4 (Long-term) and 7.24.2 (Stable)

CVE-2026-111770.description:
### Summary
In affected versions, an MCP server reached over HTTP could deliver one client's responses and notifications to another client. This happened when clients shared one stateless transport, or one `McpServer` or `Server` instance.

Messages were matched to a connection by JSON-RPC `id` alone. SDK clients number requests from 0, so ids collide in normal use.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if more than one client can reach your HTTP endpoint and your code creates the transport or the server once at startup, instead of once per request or per session. Until this release, the README examples of `@modelcontextprotocol/hono`, `express`, `fastify` and `node` showed that pattern.

Affected versions: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0.

Not affected:

- `createMcpHandler()` with a factory that builds a new server on every call
- stdio servers
- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.26.0 and later

### Fix
Upgrade to `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later.

**You also need to change your code.** The SDK now refuses to be shared, so an affected app fails requests after upgrading: a second `connect()` rejects with `ALREADY_CONNECTED`, and a stateless transport rejects its second request.

Change to one of these:

- **`createMcpHandler()`:** pass a factory that builds a new `McpServer` on every call.
- **Per request:** build a new `McpServer` and a new transport inside the request handler.
- **Per session:** set `sessionIdGenerator` and keep one `McpServer` and one transport per session.

If you cannot upgrade yet, the same change fixes affected versions.

CVE-2026-111768.description:
### Summary
In affected versions, servers put no limit on how many array elements and object keys they validated in one request. One HTTP request within the default 4 MiB size limit could exhaust the server's memory, and the process aborted with `JavaScript heap out of memory`.

No credentials are needed, unless you authenticate requests before they reach the SDK.

### Am I affected?
Yes, if clients you do not fully trust can reach your server over HTTP. The risk is highest for `McpServer` tools whose input contains an array or a record. stdio-only servers are not affected.

Affected versions:

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.3.0 through 1.31.0
- `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

### Fix
Upgrade to:

- 1.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.32.0 or later
- 2.x: `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.3.0 or later

**Upgrading alone changes nothing.** The patched versions add an `McpServer` option, `maxToolInputElements`, that is off by default. Make both of these changes:

1. Set `maxToolInputElements` just above the largest input your tools need, for example `new McpServer(info, { maxToolInputElements: 10_000 })`. It counts array elements and object keys in a call's arguments. A call over the limit gets an `isError: true` result.
2. Lower the request size limit to what your tools need. The option covers tool arguments only, and the size limit covers everything else. Set `maxRequestBodySize` on the transport or `createMcpHandler()`. If you parse the body yourself, for example with `express.json()` or Fastify, set that parser's limit.

If you cannot upgrade yet, make the second change. `maxRequestBodySize` needs `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` 1.30.1 or `@modelcontextprotocol/server` 2.1.0. Below that, use a reverse proxy.

CVE-2026-33944.description: ### Summary A SQL Injection vulnerability exists in the Third Party (Company) update functionality of Dolibarr ERP/CRM. The `localtax1_value` parameter (`lt1`) is concatenated directly into an SQL UPDATE statement in `societe/class/societe.class.php` at line 1672 without any escaping, type casting, or parameterized query binding. An authenticated user with standard "Third Party: Create/Edit" permission can extract any data from the database, including password hashes, API keys, and all business data. Tested on Dolibarr v23.0.0 (latest stable), default installation via official Docker image, MariaDB 10.11. No custom modules, no modified configuration. ### Details **Vulnerable code** (`societe/class/societe.class.php`, line 1672): ```php $sql .= ",localtax1_value =".$this->localtax1_value; ``` The value comes from `GETPOST('lt1', 'alpha')` (`societe/card.php`, line 1135). The only sanitization applied is `trim()` at line 1528 — no `(float)` cast, no `$db->escape()`. The `alpha` input filter strips HTML tags and double quotes but does **not** strip single quotes, parentheses, commas, or SQL keywords. Since the injection point is in a numeric SQL context (no quotes around the value), the attacker needs none of the filtered characters. **Why the WAF does not block this:** Dolibarr's WAF (`waf.inc.php`) only checks SQL injection patterns in **GET** parameters, not POST. The POST-based `lt1` parameter bypasses it entirely. **The same vulnerability exists** for `localtax2_value` (parameter `lt2`) at line 1682. Adjacent fields like `localtax1_assuj` are properly cast to `(int)`, showing the developers were aware of injection risk but missed these fields. ### PoC **Steps to reproduce:** 1. Install Dolibarr v23.0.0 (tested with official Docker image, MariaDB 10.11) 2. Log in with a user that has "Third Parties: Create/Edit" permission (standard user, not admin) 3. Create or open any existing Third Party (company) record 4. Click "Edit" on the company card to open the update form 5. Intercept the POST request (e.g., Burp Suite) and add these parameters to the request body: - `localtax1assuj_value=1` - `lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)` 6. Submit the form (server responds with HTTP 302 Found — successful update) 7. Navigate to the company's Notes tab — the admin's MD5 password hash is now visible in the "Private Note" field **Verification:** `echo -n "admin123" | md5sum` → `0192023a7bbd73250516f069df18b500` (matches exfiltrated hash). **Figure 1 — Notes tab before exploitation (Private Note field is empty):** **Figure 2 — Burp Suite Repeater: full POST request headers and HTTP 302 Found response:** **Figure 3 — Burp Suite Repeater: request body with injected `localtax1assuj_value=1` and `lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)`:** **Figure 4 — Notes tab after exploitation: Private Note now contains `0192023a7bbd73250516f069df18b500` (MD5 hash of admin password "admin123"):** **curl PoC:** ```bash curl -b cookies.txt \ --data-urlencode "action=update" \ --data-urlencode "token=CSRF_TOKEN" \ --data-urlencode "socid=1" \ --data-urlencode "name=TestCompany" \ --data-urlencode "status=1" \ --data-urlencode "localtax1assuj_value=1" \ --data-urlencode "lt1=1,note_private=(SELECT pass_crypted FROM llx_user WHERE rowid=1)" \ --data-urlencode "client=1" \ --data-urlencode "typent_id=0" \ "http://TARGET/societe/card.php?socid=1" ``` **Additional proof — arithmetic evaluation:** Sending `lt1=3+4` results in `localtax1_value=7.0000` stored in the database. The expression was evaluated by the SQL engine, confirming injection. **Additional proof — user count exfiltration:** Sending `lt1=(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM llx_user)` results in `localtax1_value=1.0000`. ### Impact An attacker with basic "Third Party: Create/Edit" permission (standard user, not admin) can: - **Read** any data from the database (password hashes, API keys, customer/supplier data, invoices, bank account details) - **Modify** any database record via additional SET clauses in the UPDATE injection - **Escalate** to admin by cracking MD5 password hashes (Dolibarr uses unsalted MD5 by default) - **Potentially achieve RCE** via admin features (Website module PHP injection, ModuleBuilder) after privilege escalation ### Suggested Fix ```php // societe.class.php, line 1528 — add (float) cast: $this->localtax1_value = (float) price2num(trim($this->localtax1_value)); // societe.class.php, line 1672 — add (float) cast: $sql .= ",localtax1_value =".((float) $this->localtax1_value); ``` Apply same fix for `localtax2_value` (lines 1529, 1682). ### Credit Please credit this finding to: **Grzegorz Tworek (F3715H) sec4check** (grzegorz.tworek@sec4check.pl)

Rucio is a scientific data management framework. From 1.16.1 until 35.9.0, 38.6.0, and 41.0.0rc1, the /credentials/signurl endpoint reads X-Rucio-Account instead of the account stored in request.environ['issuer'] by token authentication. Any authe...

#CVE #vulnerability #infosec #cybersecurity #security #Tenda #patchstack

CVE-2026-58273.description:
## Summary
The `/credentials/signurl` endpoint decides authorization from the client-supplied `X-Rucio-Account` HTTP header instead of the authenticated token's account. Any client holding **any** valid auth token (even a low-privilege account they legitimately own) can send `X-Rucio-Account: root` to pass the root-only permission check and have the Rucio server mint a presigned **read / write / delete** URL for an **arbitrary** object, signed with the RSE's stored S3 / GCS / Swift credentials.

## Details
`SignURL.get()` takes the authorization principal from a request header and
never uses the token-authenticated identity:

```python
# lib/rucio/web/rest/flaskapi/v1/credentials.py
account = request.headers.get('X-Rucio-Account', default=None)     # L165  (attacker-controlled)
...
result = get_signed_url(account, rse=rse, service=service,         # L194
                        operation=operation, url=url, lifetime=lifetime, vo=vo)
```

The gateway then uses that header value as the `issuer` for the permission check:

```python
# lib/rucio/gateway/credential.py
auth_result = permission.has_permission(issuer=account, vo=vo,     # L57
                                        action='get_signed_url', kwargs=kwargs, ...)
```

and the permission function is root-only:

```python
# lib/rucio/core/permission/generic.py
def perm_get_signed_url(issuer, kwargs, session):
    return _is_root(issuer)        # _is_root(x) -> x.external == 'root'
```

`InternalAccount('root', vo).external == 'root'` unconditionally, so the gate passes whenever the header is `root`. The endpoint is on `AuthenticatedBlueprint`, whose `before_request` hook validates the token and sets `request.environ['issuer']` **from the token** — but nothing ever compares `X-Rucio-Account` to it:

```python
# lib/rucio/web/rest/flaskapi/v1/common.py  (request_auth_env)
flask.request.environ['issuer'] = auth.get('account')             # L168  (the real account; unused by SignURL)
```

This is anomalous: every other authenticated handler derives the account from `request.environ['issuer']`; `credentials.py` is the only one that trusts the header. Additionally, `core.credential.get_signed_url` never checks that the supplied `url`'s host/bucket belongs to the target RSE, so even a legitimate `root` caller gets an arbitrary-object signing oracle. In multi-VO the VO is also read from the `X-Rucio-VO` header, allowing cross-tenant targeting.

## Proof of concept
Request (any valid token + spoofed account):
```
GET /credentials/signurl?rse=<cloudRSE>&svc=s3&op=delete&url=https://victim-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/important/dataset.root HTTP/1.1
X-Rucio-Auth-Token: <any valid token, even a low-privilege account>
X-Rucio-Account: root
Accept: application/octet-stream
```
Response: `200 OK` with a presigned DELETE URL the attacker replays directly against the storage backend.

## Impact
A low-privilege Rucio user can read, overwrite, and delete arbitrary objects on any cloud-backed (S3/GCS/Swift) RSE using the server's stored credentials — enabling data exfiltration, tampering, and destruction, and cross-tenant access in multi-VO deployments.

## Credit
Reported by seankohjs. Found via static analysis + manual verification.

CVE-2026-77299.description: Regexp2 is a feature-rich RegExp engine for Go. Prior to version 2.3.0, when regexp2 compiles and matches a pattern containing a large fixed-count quantifier applied to a zero-width subexpression — e.g. (?:){50000000} — the match engine executes the empty loop body m-1 times, pushing two integers onto the backtracking stack on every iteration. Because the parser accepts any repetition count up to math.MaxInt32 and the backtracking stack grows without bound, a pattern of fewer than 20 bytes matched against an empty input can force multi-gigabyte allocation and OOM-kill the process. MatchTimeout does not fully mitigate this because the memory is allocated faster than the 100 ms timeout clock can fire. This issue has been patched in version 2.3.0.

CVE-2026-83542.description:
Improper Control of Generation of Code ('Code Injection') in Apache OFBiz 24.09 before 24.09.08 on all platforms allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server by staging crafted widget XML in a multipart upload and overriding the mainDecoratorLocation used by a manager login route through an anonymous JSON request, causing OFBiz to load the staged XML through its live screen descriptor mechanism and evaluate an unsandboxed Groovy expression while rendering the authentication-failure page. Further validation established the following:

-- The exploit does not require a malformed or incomplete multipart body: a well-formed multipart request that is kept in flight and then allowed to complete normally is sufficient.

-- The screen loader reads the widget XML from a live process file descriptor while the upload is streaming, rather than from any file the attacker persists to disk.

-- The same underlying issue is also reachable through the public, explicitly unauthenticated /sfa/control/editPortalPageColumnWidth route, returning command output directly in an HTTP 200 response — it is not limited to the login-failure rendering path used in the original report.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 24.09.08, which fixes this issue.

zlib 1.4 released with the following security fixes:

- Non-blocking gzwrite() had a buffer overflow; CVE-2026-85091 (reported by mat-mo; also TOB-ZLIB-003).
- inflateGetDictionary() could write up to 8 MB past the caller's 32K buffer (Theorem THM-ZLIB-001). This took a zlib header with an invalid window size, then inflateReset() or inflateSync(). Affects 1.3.1 and 1.3.2.
- inflateSync() before the window size was known allocated a one-byte window that could later be overrun (TOB-ZLIB-004).
- inflatePrime() could lead inflate() to read before the start of the input (TOB-ZLIB-014).
- Repeated deflatePrime() calls could write past the pending buffer (TOB-ZLIB-013).
- inflateBack() failed to detect distances too far back, and copied uninitialized memory to the output (reported by Kornel Lesiński).
- gzseek() forward before any data was written could write uninitialized memory to the gzip output (found by Claude Opus 5.5).
- deflateResetKeep() used mid-stream could read outside the window (reported by Jason Gross).
- gzdopen() now sets close-on-exec with the correct flag (TOB-ZLIB-008).

https://github.com/madler/zlib/releases/tag/v1.4

#infosec #cybersecurity #CVE_2026_85091

CVE-2026-85091.description: zlib versions 1.3.1.2 through 1.3.2 contain a heap buffer overflow vulnerability in the gz_vacate() function when processing non-blocking gzwrite() operations with stale external buffer pointers. Attackers can trigger the overflow by calling gzprintf() or gzvprintf() after a write stall, causing an unchecked memmove() to write beyond the internal input buffer boundary.

CVE-2026-106069.description:
A flaw in Node.js TLS hostname verification can cause a server certificate to be validated against a different IP address than the one the client connected to, when the host is a non-canonical IPv4 literal with a leading zero, such as `0127.0.0.1`.

`tls.checkServerIdentity()` normalizes the host following the WHATWG URL rules, which read a leading-zero octet as octal (`0127.0.0.1` becomes `87.0.0.1`), while the connection is made through the operating system resolver, which on some platforms such as macOS reads it as decimal (`127.0.0.1`). A server at the connected address can then be authenticated with a certificate issued for another IP address.

This vulnerability affects Node.js **26.x**, **24.x**, and **22.x**.

In Eclipse BaSyx Helm Charts version 2.2.0 of the `aas-basyx-v2-full` chart, deployments with the bundled Keycloak enabled store the client secret of the `basyx-technical-user` OAuth2 client in cleartext in a Kubernetes ConfigMap. This client uses the client-credentials grant and its service account holds the realm `admin` role.



The chart correctly writes `keycloak.technicalUser.clientSecret` to a Kubernetes Secret, but the template `basyx-keycloak-realm.yaml` also substitutes the same value into the Keycloak realm-import JSON, which is stored in the ConfigMap `<keycloak.fullnameOverride>-realm`. A principal that can read ConfigMaps but not Secrets in the release namespace, such as a holder of the built-in Kubernetes `view` ClusterRole, can read the client secret from the ConfigMap. They can then exchange it at the Keycloak token endpoint for an access token with the `admin` role. That token grants full create, read, update, delete and execute rights on all BaSyx repositories and registries in the deployment.



The bundled Keycloak is disabled by default. No fixed release of the `aas-basyx-v2-full` chart exists. Affected users should migrate to the `basyx` chart, or deploy without the bundled Keycloak and rotate the `basyx-technical-user` client secret.

CVE-2026-123033.description: Authentication bypass in the HA heartbeat origin check in middlewared in TrueNAS SCALE before 25.10.8 (and in release trains before their respective fixes) allows an attacker on the same network segment to achieve unauthenticated full-administrator API access and execute commands as root. middlewared registers the HA peer-authentication hook (ha_permission) unconditionally, with no failover-licence or heartbeat-interface check. An unauthenticated connection whose TCP peer address is a hardcoded HA heartbeat address (169.254.10.1 or 169.254.10.2) and whose peer port is <= 1024 is granted a node credential that is authorized for every API method and treated as full administrator. Both conditions are properties of the attacker's own socket, and thus an attacker on the same layer-2 segment satisfies them without forging anything. The fix additionally requires that the connection terminate on the HA heartbeat listener (a local address/port the attacker cannot control).

CVE-2026-46300.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: skbuff: preserve shared-frag marker during coalescing

skb_try_coalesce() can attach paged frags from @from to @to.  If @from
has SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG set, the resulting @to skb can contain the same
externally-owned or page-cache-backed frags, but the shared-frag marker
is currently lost.

That breaks the invariant relied on by later in-place writers.  In
particular, ESP input checks skb_has_shared_frag() before deciding
whether an uncloned nonlinear skb can skip skb_cow_data().  If TCP
receive coalescing has moved shared frags into an unmarked skb, ESP can
see skb_has_shared_frag() as false and decrypt in place over page-cache
backed frags.

Propagate SKBFL_SHARED_FRAG when skb_try_coalesce() transfers paged
frags.  The tailroom copy path does not need the marker because it copies
bytes into @to's linear data rather than transferring frag descriptors.

#Apache #ZooKeeper #OpenOffice #ActiveMQ #Juneau #CVE2026115448 #PatchNow #Vulnerability

CVE-2026-115448.description:
Uncontrolled recursion in Apache ZooKeeper. The server serializes its data tree to a snapshot by recursing one stack frame per znode level, with no depth bound. A client permitted to create znodes (the default root ACL is open) can build a chain of nested znodes deep enough that taking a snapshot exhausts the JVM stack and kills the snapshot thread; sizes stay within jute.maxbuffer, so existing limits do not prevent it. This is a denial of service that becomes persistent: on restart the server rebuilds the deep tree from its transaction log and fails again while taking the startup snapshot, so it does not return to service, and recovery can entail data loss. The same log affects a leader and its followers, so it can spread across an ensemble.

This issue affects Apache ZooKeeper 3.8.0 through 3.8.7 and 3.9.0 through 3.9.6. Users are recommended to upgrade to 3.8.8 or 3.9.7, which fix the issue. As a workaround, use ACLs and authentication to restrict znode creation rather than relying on the default open root ACL.

CVE-2026-100252.description:
Improper Authorization vulnerability in Apache ZooKeeper.

When SASL authentication is enabled on the client port, the server's SASL callback handler grants every authorization identity (authzid) that a client requests, without checking it against the principal the client authenticated as. The server then tries to replace the requested identity with a canonical form of the authenticated principal, derived from the zookeeper.security.auth_to_local rules. If no rule applies to the principal, canonicalization fails and the error is only logged. The client-requested authzid then becomes the session's SASL identity for all ACL checks.

An authenticated client whose principal is not covered by the auth_to_local rules can therefore claim any SASL identity. With the default rules, this includes any Kerberos principal from a realm other than the server's default realm, such as a principal from a cross-realm trusted realm. The client then gets the permissions granted to that identity in sasl ACLs. If the requested identity matches a configured zookeeper.superUser, it gets superuser access to the whole data tree.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 3.8.8 or 3.9.7, which fixes the issue.

🚨 A PackageKit race condition can let a local unprivileged user gain root access on affected Linux systems; CVE-2026-41651

PoC: https://github.com/0xBlackash/CVE-2026-41651

The flaw is a time-of-check time-of-use race condition in PackageKit transaction flags. An attacker with local access can abuse the transaction state to install arbitrary packages as root, including packages containing privileged install scripts.

PackageKit | Local Privilege Escalation

CVSS: 8.8 High
Affected: PackageKit 1.0.2 through 1.3.4
Fixed: PackageKit 1.3.5
Impact: Local privilege escalation to root

The vulnerability, dubbed Pack2TheRoot, affects multiple Linux distributions and can be exploited by a local low-privileged user without additional user interaction.

🚨 A Samba printing flaw can turn a malicious print job name into remote code execution; CVE-2026-4480

PoC: https://github.com/0xBlackash/CVE-2026-4480

The vulnerability affects Samba’s printing subsystem when %J is used inside a custom print command. A client-controlled print job name can reach the shell without proper escaping, allowing shell metacharacters to alter the command being executed.

Samba Printing | Command Injection RCE

CVSS: 9.8 Critical
Affected: Samba < 4.22.10, < 4.23.8, and < 4.24.3
Fixed: Samba 4.22.10, 4.23.8, and 4.24.3
Impact: Unauthenticated remote code execution under affected configurations

The repository documents the vulnerable configuration, attack path, affected versions, detection guidance, and mitigation steps.

CVE-2026-4480.description:
A flaw was found in the Samba printing subsystem. Samba passes the client-controlled job description string to the command configured with the "print command" setting via the "%J"
substitution character without escaping shell meta characters. A remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a specially crafted print job description that contains unescaped shell characters. This could lead to remote code execution on the affected system.

posts.content:
🚨 A Linux kernel vhost flaw can let a local attacker cross virtualization boundaries and escalate privileges; CVE-2026-74580

PoC: https://github.com/YounesHfa/CVE-2026-74580

The vulnerability stems from stale vring metadata caching in the kernel’s vhost subsystem.

Reconfiguring a vring while a device IOTLB is attached can lead to out-of-bounds memory access and host kernel memory corruption.

Details

CVSS: 8.8 High
Impact: Local privilege escalation / host kernel compromise
Affected: Multiple Linux kernel versions using vulnerable vhost implementations
Fixed: Vendor-specific patched kernel releases are available

The exploit repository demonstrates the issue against multiple RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 kernel builds and includes automated checks for vulnerable kernel versions and required vhost device permissions.

CVE-2026-74580.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

vhost: reset the vring metadata cache on vring reconfiguration

vq->meta_iotlb[] caches the vhost_iotlb_map that backs each vring
metadata region, and iotlb_access_ok() returns early on a cache hit,
taking the hit as proof that the region has already been validated:

	if (vhost_vq_meta_fetch(vq, addr, len, type))
		return true;

The cache is reset on VHOST_IOTLB_UPDATE and VHOST_IOTLB_INVALIDATE, on
device IOTLB (re)initialisation and on vq reset, but not when
VHOST_SET_VRING_ADDR replaces vq->desc, vq->avail and vq->used, nor when
VHOST_SET_VRING_NUM changes the region sizes.

With a device IOTLB attached both ioctls are accepted while the vq is
live, and neither validates the addresses at ioctl time: vq_access_ok()
and vq_log_used_access_ok() return true early because the addresses are
GIOVAs, deferring validation to prefetch time.  Once the cache has been
populated that deferred validation no longer runs -- vq_meta_prefetch()
hits the stale entry and returns true -- and vhost_vq_meta_fetch() keeps
translating through the old mapping as

	map->addr + addr - map->start

for an address the mapping no longer covers.  vhost_copy_to_user() and
vhost_copy_from_user() consume the result with __copy_to_user() and
__copy_from_user(), which do not check it either, so a subsequent used
ring update or descriptor fetch accesses memory outside the region the
IOTLB actually maps.

Reset the metadata cache whenever the vring is reconfigured, so the new
addresses are pushed back through iotlb_access_ok()'s slow path.

CVE-2026-58115.description:
A vulnerability has been identified in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced (6ES7647-0BA00-1YA2) (All versions < V4.3.4-1 running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed), SIMATIC IoT2050 Basic (6ES7647-0BA00-0YA2) (All versions < V4.3.4-1 running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed), SIMATIC IoT2050 M.2 (6ES7647-0BB00-1YA2) (All versions < V4.3.4-1 running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed), SIMATIC IoT2050 SM (6ES7647-0CA00-1AA2) (All versions < V4.3.4-1 running Industrial OS with Node-RED installed). Affected devices do not enforce authentication on the Node-RED HTTP interface, allowing unauthenticated access to programming nodes that are capable of executing system commands on the server.
This could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to create malicious flows through the HTTP interface in order to execute arbitrary code on the underlying server with maximum privileges.
